title: Arrakis: How To Build An AI Sandbox From Scratch - Abhishek Bhardwaj, OpenAI

summary: Abhishek Bhardwaj introduces Arrakis, an open-source, self-hostable AI sandbox service built on microVMs for secure code execution and full computer use. His background spans CMU, Microsoft (WSL, smart watch OS), Google (containers, microVMs), and Replit, positioning Arrakis at the intersection of OS, sandboxes, and AI agents. He motivates sandboxes by noting that modern models like o3 use tool calling during inference, RL training needs sandboxed reward functions at scale, and agents benefit from full Linux environments for debugging, backtracking, and replanning. Arrakis features include sub-7-second boot, fast snapshots, port forwarding, pre-installed Chrome with VNC, Python SDK, Golang CLI, MCP server, OpenAPI YAML, and Docker-based customization. The talk provides a Linux sandboxing primer covering thread-based execution, containers as namespaces and cgroups, and their shared-kernel security weakness. Container hardening via Linux capabilities, seccomp filters, and mini jail reduces but does not eliminate the attack surface, motivating the shift to virtualization. In Linux virtualization, a VMM like QEMU, crosvm, or firecracker sits on top of /dev/kvm, spawning VMs with their own guest kernel and user space for stronger isolation. MicroVMs (crosvm, firecracker, cloud hypervisor) are written in Rust for memory safety, jail emulated devices separately, support fewer architectures and devices, and boot faster with less memory. Arrakis chose Cloud Hypervisor for its hot plugging of devices, GPU support, snapshot support, and governance independence. For storage, Arrakis uses an overlay FS with a shared read-only base layer across sandboxes and a per-sandbox read-write layer, protecting the root FS from deletion attacks while enabling efficient snapshot persistence of only the read-write layer. For networking, each sandbox gets a unique tap device connected to a Linux bridge on the host, with port forwarding handled via iptables DNAT rules so VNC clients and code servers are accessible from the host. Docker customization allows users to modify a Dockerfile based on Ubuntu 22.04 with pre-installed Chrome, NodeJS, npm, and Python. VM creation in code allocates vCPUs as host threads, calculates memory as a fraction of host memory, creates networking devices, and spawns a VMM process via the create VM API. A bundled code execution server provides files upload/download and command execution APIs returning JSON output or error, running safely inside the guest VM. Snapshotting motivation is that agents fail on large multi-step tasks and should backtrack to a last good checkpoint, replan, and retry, or explore multiple paths in parallel for more reliable results. The snapshot workflow has four steps: pause the VM via the VMM pause API, call snapshot to dump guest memory, manually persist the thin read-write overlay FS out of band, and resume the VMM. The Python SDK offers a dead-simple API: pip install Arrakis, self-host on your infrastructure, list all VMs, start sandbox, run commands, snapshot with an ID, restore by VM name and snapshot ID, and destroy when done. A Claude Desktop demo shows it creating a collaborative Google Docs clone inside an Arrakis sandbox via the MCP server, adding dark mode, then restoring an earlier snapshot to remove it—all with minimal prompting. Ongoing work targets sub-1-second boot times, first-class snapshot persistence by moving from ext4 to btrfs for native incremental snapshots, and dynamic memory management via ballooning or hot plugging/removal of memory to maximize sandbox density per server. The talk concludes with Abhishek thanking the audience and offering to help anyone with questions.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Speaker Background and Motivation for AI Sandboxes
sections.summary: Abhishek introduces himself and his background at CMU, Microsoft (WSL, smart watch OS), Google (containers, microVMs), and Replit. He explains why AI sandboxes are needed: tool calling in modern models like o3, RL reward functions at scale, agent debugging and backtracking with full Linux environments, and security against buggy or malicious AI-generated code.

sections.title: Introducing Arrakis and Its Features
sections.summary: Arrakis is presented as an open-source, self-hostable microVM-based sandbox service with backtracking via snapshot/restore. Features include sub-7-second boot, fast snapshots, port forwarding, pre-installed Chrome with VNC, Python SDK, Golang CLI, MCP server, OpenAPI YAML, and Docker-based customization. A Manas AI demo is shown.

sections.title: Arrakis Architecture and API
sections.summary: The high-level architecture includes a REST server managing microVM sandboxes with VNC and code-server, port forwarding, Python SDK, Golang CLI, and MCP server. The REST API exposes VMs, snapshots, command execution, file upload/download, and health check endpoints. The system is tied to Linux via /dev/kvm.

sections.title: Linux Sandboxing Primer: Execution Model and Containers
sections.summary: Begins a deep dive into Linux sandboxing. Covers the thread-based execution model (task structs, scheduler run queues, processes as thread groups sharing page tables, kernel privileged access via system calls). Then explains containers as collections of namespaces (process, mount, net) with cgroups for resource limits, and their security weakness: containers share the host kernel as native processes, so kernel vulnerabilities can be exploited for root access.

sections.title: Container Hardening and Linux Virtualization
sections.summary: Explains techniques to reduce container attack surface: Linux capabilities, seccomp filters, and the mini jail library from Chrome OS. Notes that jail techniques have limits and can still be bypassed. Transitions to virtualization as a heavier hammer: each VM has its own guest user space and guest kernel, providing a smaller attack surface to the host kernel. Dives into Linux virtualization mechanics: the VMM process sits on /dev/kvm, spawns VMs, manages emulated devices, and handles VM exits when the guest needs host resources, then resumes the guest. CPU-bound guest code runs with near-zero penalty but I/O-heavy workloads suffer from frequent VM exits.

sections.title: MicroVMs and VMM Selection for Arrakis
sections.summary: Explains microVMs: Rust-based VMMs (crosvm, firecracker, cloud hypervisor) that provide memory safety, jail emulated devices separately, support fewer architectures and devices, and thus boot faster with less memory. Arrakis chose microVMs for multi-tenant security and fast snapshotting. Compares VMMs and explains why Cloud Hypervisor was chosen for hot plugging, GPU support, snapshot support, and independent governance. G Visor is noted as a middle ground with easier GPU access but weaker isolation.

sections.title: Storage and File System Architecture
sections.summary: Covers the storage layer inside each sandbox. The threat of malicious or buggy code deleting important files motivates root FS protection. Arrakis uses an overlay FS with a shared read-only base layer across sandboxes and a per-sandbox read-write layer for new files. When snapshotting, only the read-write layer is persisted. The init script inside the guest sets up the overlay FS, so the sandbox sees a normal root mount path.

sections.title: Networking Architecture and Port Forwarding
sections.summary: Each sandbox gets a unique tap device (virtual network interface) connected to a Linux bridge on the host. Port forwarding from the host to the code server and VNC server inside the sandbox is handled via iptables DNAT rules. Code snippets show bridge device creation, firewall rules for forwarding data between host and sandbox, and port forwarding setup using Linux iptables commands. A VNC client on a laptop can access the GUI via the VNC server running inside the sandbox.

sections.title: Docker Customization and VM Creation in Code
sections.summary: Docker-based customization uses a Dockerfile based on Ubuntu 22.04 with pre-installed standard packages including Chrome (booted via systemd), NodeJS, npm, and Python. VM creation in code creates all devices: root FS with overlay FS writable path, vCPUs as host threads, memory calculated as a fraction of host memory, networking tap device, and a VMM process spawned via the create VM API with the configuration.

sections.title: Code Execution Server and Snapshotting
sections.summary: A bundled code execution server provides a files API for upload/download and a command API that executes commands and returns output or error as JSON. Running inside a guest VM provides confidence against escape. Chrome is pre-installed with port forwarding to the VNC server. Snapshotting motivation: agents fail on large multi-step tasks and should backtrack to a last good checkpoint, replan, and retry, or explore multiple paths in parallel. Snapshots save guest memory and the read-write overlay layer, restoring all processes and GUI state. Plans to move from ext4 to btrfs for native incremental snapshots.

sections.title: Snapshot Workflow and Python SDK
sections.summary: The snapshot workflow has four steps: pause the VM via the VMM pause API, call snapshot to dump guest memory, manually persist the thin read-write overlay FS out of band, and resume the VMM. Code shows pausing, creating a copy of the stateful disk (read-write overlay), calling snapshot to dump guest memory, and ensuring resume before exiting. The Python SDK offers pip install, self-hosting on your infrastructure, list all VMs, start sandbox, run command, snapshot with ID, restore by VM name and snapshot ID, and destroy.

sections.title: Claude Desktop Demo and Ongoing Work
sections.summary: Claude Desktop demo creates a collaborative Google Docs clone inside an Arrakis sandbox via the MCP server with real-time collaboration enabled by networking. A snapshot is taken, dark mode is added, then the earlier snapshot is restored to remove dark mode. The demo shows end-to-end app creation with minimal prompting and real collaboration versus fake client-side codegen. Ongoing work: sub-1-second boot times, btrfs for incremental snapshots, and dynamic memory management via ballooning or hot plugging/removal to maximize sandbox density per server.

sections.title: Closing Remarks
sections.summary: Abhishek thanks the audience and offers to help anyone with questions, closing the talk.

limitations: Arrakis is tied to Linux because the microVM technology relies on /dev/kvm
Containers share the host kernel, making them vulnerable to kernel vulnerabilities that can grant root access
Container hardening via capabilities and seccomp filters can still be bypassed
VM exits and resumes create performance overhead for I/O-heavy workloads in virtualization
MicroVMs support fewer architectures and devices than traditional VMs like QEMU
G Visor still allows untrusted code to attack the host kernel, offering weaker isolation than microVMs
Arrakis currently uses ext4 for the file system, which is not optimized for incremental snapshots; plans to move to btrfs are ongoing
Dynamic memory management and resource management for maximizing sandbox density per server is still ongoing work
